Federal Judge Dismisses Donald Trump's $10 Billion Defamation Lawsuit Against Wall Street Journal

Court Ruling Overview

A U.S. federal judge has dismissed for a second time a $10 billion defamation lawsuit filed by President Donald Trump against The Wall Street Journal. U.S. District Judge Darrin P. Gayles, presiding in Miami, ruled that the lawsuit failed to meet the legal requirements to proceed, issuing a dismissal with prejudice, which prevents the case from being refiled.

Background of the Dispute

The litigation stemmed from a report published by the newspaper last year regarding an alleged birthday letter linked to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. According to the reporting, the document, which purportedly featured Trump's name, was included in a 2003 birthday album associated with Epstein and was allegedly collected by British socialite Ghislaine Maxwell. Trump has denied authoring the letter, labeling the report as defamatory.

Key Legal Findings

  • Actual Malice Requirement: Judge Gayles determined that the complaint did not sufficiently demonstrate "actual malice," a standard established by the 1964 Supreme Court ruling in *New York Times Co. v. Sullivan*. This standard requires public figures to prove that a publication acted with reckless disregard for the truth or knowingly published false information.
  • Judicial Criticism: In his ruling, the judge described the arguments presented in the amended complaint as "grasping at straws," noting that the allegations provided were "conclusory, vague, and sometimes inconsistent."
  • Contextual Reporting: The court highlighted that The Wall Street Journal had included Trump’s denial within its original reporting, undermining the argument that the publication ignored the president's position on the matter.

Practical Implications

This decision marks the final dismissal of this specific case in the district court. While the ruling precludes Trump from refiling the same complaint in that court, legal analysts note that his legal team retains the option to challenge the decision through the appellate court system. This case is part of a broader series of legal interactions between the president and various media organizations regarding reporting and press coverage.

How to Verify

Interested parties can review the official ruling by accessing the public docket for the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida or by searching for the case file under the relevant parties on the PACER (Public Access to Court Electronic Records) database.
